name: Ovagen
lead: Ovagen is a synthetic tripeptide with the sequence Glu-Asp-Leu (EDL), developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia as part of its Cytogen family of short peptides, according to Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia [1]. It is described there as investigated for effects on the liver and gastrointestinal tract and as modulating gene expression in a tissue-specific way [1].

The same source states that evidence is limited to animal models, cell cultures and studies from Russian institutions, that no large Western randomised trials exist, and that it is marketed as a research compound or supplement rather than an approved drug [1]. Verified peer-reviewed human studies of Ovagen could not be identified.

paras: Grokipedia gives the molecular formula as C15H25N3O8 and describes the peptide as chemically synthesised, with proposed DNA binding and effects on chromatin and methylation [1]. These mechanisms are hypotheses from the developing group and the source is not independent.

card.summary: Khavinson liver-targeted tripeptide (EDL) with essentially no verifiable published human data and no appearance use.
card.note: Very thin sourcing; not an appearance product.

quick.overview:
Ovagen is a three-amino-acid peptide (Glu-Asp-Leu) developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia and described as targeting liver and gut tissue.

Verified published studies on it are scarce, and none address appearance.
quick.mechanism: Its developers propose that short peptides bind DNA and regulate gene expression; this has not been confirmed independently.
quick.risks: No human safety data could be verified. It is sold as a research compound or supplement and is not an approved drug in most countries.
